question: “Is it better to travel alone?” “It depends.” Which words could naturally come next?
choices: No, never. I won’t even take a bus on my own.
Yes, definitely. I feel exactly the same about every trip.
For a weekend, yes. For a long trip, I’d like company.
Yes, always. Travelling with people is a waste of time.
note: “It depends” prepares the listener for different answers in different situations. “Definitely” signals a much firmer answer.

picture.alt: A travel suitcase with a blank tag.

question: “The sports centre costs too much.” “I see your point.” What has the second person said so far?
choices: They promise to lower the price.
They’ve decided to leave the centre.
They know exactly what the centre costs.
They understand the reason for the complaint.
note: “I see your point” recognises a reason. The speaker can still go on to give a different opinion.

question: “That café is expensive. To be fair, the coffee is excellent.” Why does the speaker add “to be fair”?
choices: To mention a good point as well.
To ask what a fair price would be.
To check whether the bill is correct.
To report what the owner believes.
note: “To be fair” brings in a point the first comment left out. “How much should they charge?” would open a discussion about a fair price.

question: “My phone saves me time. For instance…” Which ending does the speaker’s phrase introduce?
choices: I think it saves me time in lots of ways.
I can buy my train ticket on the way to the station.
That’s my view, anyway. What do you think?
Some people would disagree with that, of course.
note: “For instance” promises an example. “In lots of ways” repeats the main idea without showing one.

picture.alt: A laptop with a blank screen.

question: “Let’s make the library open all night. On second thoughts, midnight is late enough.” What happened?
choices: The speaker agreed to decide the next night.
Someone asked the speaker for a second idea.
The speaker thought again and changed the idea.
Someone else made the speaker repeat the idea.
note: “On second thoughts” signals that the speaker has reconsidered. “What do you think?” would ask somebody else for a view.

picture.alt: A clock beside a blank calendar.

question: “Should there be a quiet floor in our library?” You say yes. “Why?” your partner asks. Conversations make it hard for you to read. What do you add?
choices: I think the quiet floor would be a really good idea.
Did you know our library already has three floors?
Well, that’s just the way I feel about quiet floors.
When people chat near me, I keep reading the same line.
note: Reading the same line shows what the problem feels like. Calling the idea good repeats your opinion when your partner has asked for a reason.

picture.alt: An open storybook with a little castle rising from its pages.

question: “Everyone should put their phones away in class,” says Ben. You agree during discussions, but your class uses phones to record interviews. What do you say?
choices: During discussions, yes. What about when we record interviews?
That could help. Shall we make a rule for the whole day?
I see. How many interviews did we record last term?
Would it help if we asked the teacher to keep everyone’s phones?
note: “During discussions, yes” keeps the part you agree with. The interview question gives Ben a real case to consider.

picture.alt: A laptop with a blank screen.

question: Your partner says, “Playing sport helps people make friends.” You met your closest friend at football practice. She asks, “Has that ever happened to you?” What do you say?
choices: Some people prefer going running or swimming on their own.
Yes. I met my best friend while we were waiting to play.
Yes. Football teams need a lot of players to do well.
I think most people would agree that sport is sociable.
note: A personal example answers “Has that happened to you?” The point about most people would fit a question about public opinion.

question: You wanted scooters off campus because they block doors. A classmate suggests parking spaces away from entrances. That solves your main concern. What do you say?
choices: I hadn’t thought of that. Which door do you usually use?
That’s worth discussing. Shall we ask for another meeting?
That could work. It was the blocked doors I was worried about.
That’s interesting. I still think all scooters should go.
note: “That could work” changes your position and tells your classmate why. “Nobody has ever had trouble” would take back the problem itself.

question: “Recorded music is better than live music,” says your partner. You love concerts, but first you want to understand her view. What do you say?
choices: Do you agree that concerts are much more exciting?
Would you like to listen to my favourite live album?
Shall we list the things we both like about music?
What do you prefer about listening to a recording?
note: “What do you prefer about…?” invites a reason in her own words. Asking her to agree about concerts puts your opinion into her answer.

question: “Cycling is the fastest way to get to class,” you say. A classmate lives across the city and takes a train. You realise you were thinking of your own short trip. What do you add?
choices: I mean for people near campus, like me.
That’s helpful. Shall we compare train ticket prices?
Fair point. I’ll try the train myself next week.
Would you like me to show you my cycle route?
note: “For people near campus” narrows the claim to the journey you know. Offering your cycle route would help someone making a similar journey, but your classmate lives much farther away.

picture.alt: A bicycle and a pink cycling jersey.

question: Your friend likes the new canteen menu because it’s cheap. You’re pleased about the price too, but there’s little you can eat as a vegetarian. What do you say?
choices: It is good value. Shall we go there again tomorrow?
It’s cheap. I wish there were more meat-free dishes.
Could we compare it with the café across the road?
I’m glad you like it. What do you usually order?
note: You agree about the price and explain the missing choice. Comparing cafés could help you find lunch, but it leaves your view of this menu unclear.

question: Someone asks if the new night bus is popular. You’ve used it once, on a Friday, and it was full. What can you say from that trip?
choices: It looked popular. I’d expect it to be full every night.
Would you like to catch it together this Friday?
It was full on Friday. I’m not sure about other nights.
I’d ask someone who uses it often before saying anything.
note: One crowded ride supports a claim about Friday. Asking a regular passenger could give you more information, but you can already share your own limited experience.

picture.alt: A red London bus beside a streetlamp.

question: The drama club can have a small room every week or a big room once a month. You need regular practice before a show. The chair asks which you prefer and why. What do you say?
choices: The big one. There’d be more room for the audience.
Either room could work. How much space do they have?
The small one is free every week, and the big one once a month.
The small one. Meeting every week matters more for this show.
note: The weekly room meets the need you named. The point about the audience would count more if you were choosing where to perform.

picture.alt: An empty stage framed by red curtains.

question: Your group is discussing video games. Two people have spoken. Mel hasn’t, and you don’t know her opinion. What do you say?
choices: Mel, how does it look to you?
Mel, you agree with us, don’t you?
Mel, shall I give your example for you?
Mel, why don’t you like video games?
note: “How does it look to you?” leaves Mel free to agree, disagree or bring up another point. Asking why she dislikes games assumes an opinion she hasn’t given.
